His tenure as President marks his fourth tenure in the Association, having previously served as Vice President, Sports Secretary, and Assistant Sports Secretary. Across these roles, he has been actively involved in student leadership, sports development, institutional engagement, and the advancement of initiatives that strengthen the AMSUL community.

Beyond student leadership, Adeleke has a strong interest in medicine, with particular interests in Orthopaedic Surgery, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Sports Medicine, and Interventional Radiology. He is also passionate about medical research, leadership development, mentorship, and creating opportunities that connect medical students with professionals and institutions locally and internationally.

As President, he is committed to strengthening AMSUL's legacy, expanding opportunities for its members, fostering stronger alumni and institutional relationships, and promoting excellence in medical education, leadership, and service.

In this capacity, he is focused on building on AMSUL's legacy, creating opportunities for its members, and advancing excellence in medical education, leadership, and service.

executives.name: Oluwatofunmi O. Apata

content.text: A two-week programme of service and development

The 59th AMSUL Health Week ran from 1 to 14 November 2025. Its programme brought together community health activity, academic competition, career development, entrepreneurship, research and student recognition. The report presents the week as both a celebration of AMSUL’s legacy and a platform for extending its work across the College and wider community.
Across the programme, the report records nearly ₦4 million in prizes and awards, alongside participation from students, schools, health professionals, community members and programme partners.
Community health and outreach

The Health Walk and Medical Outreach centred on Surulere Public Library. The four-hour outreach, held from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., reached 300 community members and involved 70 volunteers. Fifty AMSULites also took part in “Stride Against Hypertension.” Health education was delivered in Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, with clinical services including blood-pressure checks, Hepatitis B and C screening, full blood count testing, eye examinations and free glasses.

The report recognizes more than 12 partners and sponsors connected with this outreach, including ARISE Women Nigeria and the Lagos Doyen Lions Club. The combination of local-language education, screening and referral activity placed student volunteers alongside community participants and health partners.
Learning, enterprise and academic exchange

The Business Summit brought together 300 attendees, eight contestants and six sponsors. Its activities included the Kakaride Challenge, with a ₦50,000 prize, and an elevator-pitch competition, with a ₦100,000 prize. IdeaTrophy involved seven teams of three to six members and a 30-day mentorship roadmap covering innovation, epidemic control in low- and middle-income countries, technology, pitching, market fit and scalability.

The intercollegiate quiz and debate programme connected nine schools across Nigeria, Uganda, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Qatar and the United States. AMSUL won the Nigerian Inter-MSA preliminary and placed third in the intercontinental final, behind Zimbabwe and Qatar. The report also documents a separate Professor Durosimi-Etti Intercollegiate Quiz.
Professional development and recognition

Career Day created space for specialty exploration, career planning, a keynote address and breakout mentorship. The Scientific Conference focused on research, innovation and global-health perspectives. The closing dinner brought together 155 AMSULites and presented 18 awards; the report records two Benzene Awards for Academic Excellence, with ₦200,000 awarded in each of the preclinical and clinical categories.

Taken together, the documented activities connect community-facing health work with student learning, professional exchange and collaboration across institutions. The report provides a record of the people, partners and programme formats that made that reach possible.
Two programmes for women’s health and leadership

AMSUL’s International Women’s Day 2026 programme brought together a community outreach in Mushin and a conference on women’s leadership in healthcare. The report frames the activities around access to health information, preventive care, empowerment, mentorship and participation in more equitable healthcare systems.

The outreach took place at Mushin Market on 7 March under the theme “The Wellness Pavilion: Investing Where the Need is Greatest.” The conference followed on 14 March under the theme “Empowered Now, Leading Tomorrow: Preparing Women to Lead Equitable Healthcare Systems.”
Health engagement in Mushin

The outreach included an awareness walk through the market, health talks, screenings, consultations, medicine dispensing and referrals. The report records 272 women reached and 150 people receiving health education, with four doctors involved. Screening covered five categories: blood pressure, blood glucose, Hepatitis B, breast examination and body-mass-index checks.
The format brought preventive-health information and basic screening into the market setting, with opportunities for consultation and referral alongside community education.
A conference on leadership in healthcare

The conference recorded 329 attendees and featured keynote contributions from Dr Samantha Tross and Professor Modupe Elebute-Odunsi, alongside talks by Pastor Siju Iluyomade and Mrs Beatrice Eneh. The programme also included a piano performance by Miss T’mara O., spoken word by Emifah Eforme-Bello, “Becoming Her: Women Stepping into Influence,” and a secondary-school speech competition on women’s leadership.
Together, the programme elements linked professional perspectives with creative expression, mentorship and opportunities for younger participants to speak about leadership.
Recognized partners and documented reach

The report lists CLP Legal, Nigerian Bottling Company, SOG Concepts, Smoothie Daddy, Nectar Beauty Hub, Ursula Scents Collection, Zaimak Prints & Gifts, and Marcelle Ruth Cancer Center and Specialist Hospital among its sponsors. It does not assign specific contributions to each organization, so they are recognized here as listed in the report.

Across the two dates, the report documents community health engagement, medical participation and a conference that drew students, guests and secondary-school participants. This record shows how the association’s women’s-health and leadership work brought community activity and wider healthcare conversations into the same programme.

It’s a hot, blistering Tuesday, the clinic has been running since 9a.m and at 2p.m, exhaustion is palpable among you and your classmates. Waiting for the next patient to come in, your consultant tries to lift the mood, by asking each of you about what they plan to specialize in.

As you listen to your classmates give amazing answers, which start to pique your interest, you stand up a little straighter, eager to listen to their answers. One person says orthopaedic surgery, he explains that he really connected with the specialty while he rotated through it and nothing else interested him as much as it did. You nod your head, ‘that’s very sensible’ you think. The next person says oncology, they explain how a relative of theirs died of cancer and the reason they got into medicine was so they could do some cancer research, you sympathize with them. Another classmate responds ‘I think I’d like to specialize in dermatology, it’s always fascinated me how there aren’t a lot of dermatologists in the country, but the largest organ in the body is the skin, it just doesn’t add up’, she says.

Finally, the spotlight lands on you. Everyone is looking, waiting. You search for an answer, but the silence continues and stretches for over a minute, broken only by the entry of the next patient. And that’s when it hits you, you have no idea what you want to specialize in.

So you look up at your consultant and smile weakly ‘I don’t know sir’, you eventually mutter. ‘Well that’s okay’ he assures you, not everybody knows what they want to do’. Despite the reassurance, a seed of doubt has been planted. Why is everyone else so certain and why are you so different? This uncertainty persists even long after you have left the clinic.
How do you choose just one path out of so many? How do you know which choice is best and how do you ensure you won’t regret it?
If this story resonates with you, keep reading.
This interview is with Dr Olopade, a renowned endocrinology consultant who, as a medical student, was equally undecided about his future specialty.
CLINICAL ROTATIONS AND SPECIALTY INFLUENCES DURING MEDICAL SCHOOL
The Interview with Dr Olopade

“In medical school, I rotated through all the core postings. However, I quickly ruled out pediatrics. My reason was the diagnostic challenge: I couldn’t understand how doctors could arrive at a diagnosis when their patients, who could only cry, were unable to express themselves. This perceived difficulty made me decide against the specialty.”
He however enjoyed both of his rotations in surgery and medicine, though there were further perceived difficulties during the medicine posting.

“During my medicine rotation, I felt quite conflicted because multiple physicians would offer two or three different diagnoses for the same patient. This made me question the stability of the medicine specialty, it seemed as though the specialty was ‘upside down’ as everyone had a unique, and confusing, diagnosis. Consequently, I gravitated more toward surgery in medical school, because in surgery, a swelling is definitively a swelling, and the required action is clear: remove it.”
Dr Olopade then talks about how some of his lecturers made some valuable impact in his decision making process.

“II had two standout physicians during my training. One was a gastroenterologist whose teaching style was unique. The other was a nephrologist who introduced a different dimension to medical education, making me realize that medicine wasn’t so bad; it presented a real opportunity for learning. What particularly drew me in was the ease with which I could grasp the material I was studying.”
It wasn’t until final year that a decision was made and even then, uncertainty still lingered.

“I remained undecided about my specialty until I completed the final year (600 level) of my MBBS program. In the final exams, I performed well in both medicine and surgery. Although I struggled with the long case in surgery, I achieved one of the best results in the short case. At that time, we had the traditional four-stage exam, and all stages were mandatory to pass.
Even after medical school, I was still torn between medicine and surgery.

My decision was influenced by two key factors. While assisting with surgery as a medical student, I frequently experienced needle pricks. When I researched this, I came across a case where a surgeon contracted hepatitis and was advised to stop operating. This was a deal-breaker for me, as a surgeon who cannot operate is fundamentally limited. Although I had initially considered becoming an orthopedic surgeon, this experience made me reconsider.
Secondly, a cardiologist shared a piece of advice that resonated with me: 60% to 70% of hospital patients are medical cases. This observation is verifiable and confirmed my lean toward medicine.”
THE EUREKA MOMENT; WHAT DREW HIM IN?

“I had wonderful teachers in medical school, although most were cardiologists, nephrologists, neurologists, and pulmonologists. I never had an endocrinologist as a teacher, so that field wasn’t even on my radar. After graduation, I felt I was well-suited to be a cardiologist because I found it easy to identify murmurs, listen to heart sounds, and perform examinations.

However, during my house job before residency, two people significantly influenced my path. I spent about three months with a pulmonologist. Though he wasn’t actively teaching me, he supervised my work.

Later, during my medicine posting at a different center, I encountered a gastroenterologist, Dr. O. He conducted ward rounds with me four times a week as a consultant. This interaction deepened my interest in internal medicine and significantly improved my thoroughness. Ultimately, my enjoyment of this posting made me aspire to become a gastroenterologist like him.”
However, these weren’t the only people who Dr Olopade drew inspiration from.

”There was another professor, professor A, a nephrologist, the man was “rolling stuff”. He. made me feel I could be a nephrologist. At this time, my decision was to either be a nephrologist or a gastroenterologist.

So after passing my primary exams, I had intended to pursue a specialization in gastroenterology. My rotations in medicine included about six different postings. Interestingly, I had not completed an endoscopy posting before sitting for my Part 1 exam. Unfortunately, I failed that exam by a single mark.”

Failing an exam is something many of us have dealt with, it was reassuring to discover that even our infallible and highly renowned consultants were truly once students. How did Dr Olopade deal with this?

“Failing Part I of the exam meant a mandatory six-month waiting period before I could retake it. This unexpected gap turned out to be an opportunity, allowing me to finally complete an endocrinology posting, a specialty I had never experienced before.”
He saw an opportunity in the situation, one that led him to where he is today.

“A significant event occurred during that Part I exam. While the teachers in the gastroenterology department knew I was interested in their specialty, they offered no support after my failure. Instead, the people who genuinely comforted me were the endocrinologists — even though I hadn’t even done their posting yet.

When I finally started the endocrinology posting, the staff made the experience easy, enjoyable, and something I could love. I realized that endocrinology required brushing up on biochemistry, anatomy, and physiology, which felt relatable and came easily to me because of my prior knowledge.

My takeaway is this: A specialty must be something that comes to you naturally, something you genuinely enjoy, and something you will never get bored of, as it will be your life’s work. It’s best to let your true calling emerge naturally. For me, I found endocrinology easy to connect with.
Consequently, immediately after passing my Part I exam, I made up my mind on endocrinology. Even when the gastroenterology people eventually came calling, my mind was already made up.”
DECISION MADE; WHAT NEXT?
Navigating the next steps

“My first step was to approach the endocrinology faculty and teachers to share my intentions and I was warmly received by Professor A.O., the lead professor and the acknowledged doyen at the time, who was responsible for training most of Nigeria’s endocrinologists.

He welcomed me and two of my colleagues. At the time, an endocrinology rotation was usually avoided, primarily because being on the endocrine posting meant meeting with the professor four times a week.”
The hours were rigorous but he was willing to put in the work.
“The schedule runs from morning to night so some days you are in the department till 7pm, others as late 10pm on the days when we had to write abstracts in preparation for upcoming conferences.

However, I did not mind doing all of that with my professor because he was very thorough so I just made up my mind that the next 3 years would be solely dedicated to endocrinology and ensured I met all the requirements to qualify for my part two exam.
I think I was ready for the exam even before the scheduled date.”
WAS THERE ANY ADVICE FROM YOUR CONSULTANTS THAT YOU WOULD LIKE TO PASS ON?

“Funnily enough, there wasn’t any major advice I was specifically given, but the most important lesson I’ve held onto is the need to be genuinely motivated by what you choose. I always say: do what truly interests you, not something you’ll end up regretting later. What comes naturally to you is usually what you should pursue. Also consider what you enjoy doing consistently without getting burnt out, because if you know you get bored easily, that field may not be the right fit.

When choosing a specialty, think long term. If you don’t see yourself in that space in the next five years, then it may not be for you. If you can’t picture yourself there, don’t do it. It’s also important to remember that specialization is not compulsory, there are many other career paths available. You can be a clinical teacher or a scientist without necessarily being a practicing clinician. Many people assume they must remain clinicians, but that isn’t the only option. You can even be in endocrinology without being a clinician.

Ultimately, choose what comes naturally to you, something that excites you when you see cases and makes you want to help patients. If it doesn’t excite you, it may not be worth pursuing. One essential mindset in any specialty you choose is the willingness to continually grow and advance your career.”
WORK LIFE BALANCE
What can you say about work life balance when it comes to choosing a specialty?

“For example, I initially loved surgery, but I had to ask myself whether I wanted to spend my entire career in the theatre. I also enjoyed my O&G posting, it came easily to me, but I felt it was too narrow for the kind of challenge I wanted. I needed something that would constantly engage my thinking, where finding solutions would directly improve patients’ lives. I always say that any specialty you choose should leave people better off after they’ve seen you; not as a place of conflict, but one of healing and hope. As clinicians, we are here to improve quality of life and restore hope.

When I considered surgery, I also reflected on practical aspects such as the long hours in theatre and even personal experiences like needle pricks, which influenced my thinking. I felt I would be better suited as a physician than as a surgeon. Additionally, many surgeons deal with issues like low back pain due to prolonged standing and bending in theatre, and I also valued a role where I could have more direct control over patient management, rather than depending heavily on multiple team factors for outcomes.

I also appreciated that as a physician, I could apply my skills more readily in everyday life — for example, being able to assist family members in medical situations, such as managing a stroke or recognising hypothyroidism when others had missed it.
This is what I considered regarding work-life balance.
Eventually, I chose a specialty where I could consistently apply my knowledge to help my family, my patients, and my wider community.”
MONEY, CAREER LONGEVITY, JOB AVAILABILITY
How did factors like income, job prospect and training length influence your decision?

“I didn’t really consider income when making my decision. Over time, I’ve come to realize that it is better to pursue honour in your journey in life rather than focusing primarily on money. When you focus on doing things with integrity and becoming the best version of yourself as a doctor, money will eventually come as a natural result. However, if you chase money directly, you may achieve it, but it can come at the cost of dissatisfaction or even compromising your values.

In medicine, there is a need to always uphold dignity in practice. So for me, money was not the major driving factor. I would rather focus on becoming a good doctor and maintaining integrity. One of the key lessons I learned from my anatomy professor is that ‘life is interesting to those who have made it interesting for themselves’. That really stayed with me. It reminded me that you should focus on building a meaningful and fulfilling career rather than just chasing financial gain.

Of course, in our context, especially in Nigeria, remuneration may not always reflect the effort required. But I strongly believe that if you do your work well, focus on excellence, and pursue honour in your practice, the financial rewards will eventually follow.”
LIKES AND DISLIKES IN THE CHOSEN SPECIALTY
What do you like or dislike so far in endocrinology?
“What I like most about endocrinology is the opportunity it gives me to help patients through careful diagnosis and finding solutions to complex conditions.

However, one of the challenges I’ve observed is the limitation in access to proper investigations. Endocrinology often requires both basal and dynamic tests to reach a definitive diagnosis, but many of these investigations are expensive and not easily accessible to patients. The cost of laboratory tests and even the materials required can be beyond what most patients can afford. Unfortunately, health insurance coverage does not always support these advanced dynamic tests, which can be quite frustrating clinically because it limits how much help we can offer.

In addition, the cost of medications is also a major challenge, as many of the treatments are not affordable for a large proportion of our patients. This can sometimes make it difficult to provide optimal care despite having the knowledge and tools to do so.”
REFLECTIONS
Is there anything you would have done differently?

“I don’t have any regrets; however, I would have liked to take up a lecturing role because I enjoy teaching. Unfortunately, due to certain circumstances, that wasn’t possible. That’s the only thing I would say I might have done differently.”
PARTING ADVICE FOR FUTURE DOCTORS
What would you like to say to the undecided medical students?

“One important piece of advice is to take every posting seriously and actively identify what you can learn from it. Pay attention to what comes naturally to you in each rotation, what excites you, and even what your fears are in different postings. For example, during my paediatric posting, one of my challenges was understanding the way doctors communicated with both children and their parents. It didn’t come naturally to me, and that helped me realise I was less inclined towards paediatric endocrinology. In O&G, I found the scope a bit too narrow and not as intellectually challenging as I wanted. In contrast, I found medicine both challenging and exciting, and that is what ultimately led me into the field.

Secondly, once you find a specialty that interests you, make an effort to understand it deeply. Join interest groups, participate in specialty societies, and attend conferences and academic programmes. The limited duration of clinical rotations may not be enough to fully appreciate a specialty or decide on a career path. Being actively involved helps you gain better clarity. Even the development of student or interest clubs can play an important role in nurturing future specialists.”
Rooting for you always! 🤍 — AMSUL Editorial board, 2026.

Dr. Erere Otrofanowei is one of the most remarkable individuals you will ever encounter. It was with a warm and earnest demeanor that she welcomed us into her office at Lagos University Teaching Hospital, instantly putting us at ease.

A consultant dermatologist and senior lecturer at the College of Medicine, University of Lagos, Dr. Otrofanowei also serves on the board of the African Society of Dermatology and Venereology and is a international fellow of the American Academy of Dermatologists. Her office walls tell her story, a rich tapestry of newspaper clippings, awards, and recognitions — but perhaps the most memorable feature is a quaint cuckoo clock that chimes on the hour, a piece that somehow makes perfect sense once you get to know her.

Before we began, she congratulated the association and commended our efforts to guide future doctors. It set the tone for a conversation that ranged from the heart of dermatology to pressing issues in the field.
The interview, conducted in July to mark UV Safety Awareness Month, has been lightly edited for clarity while preserving her authentic voice.
Why Dermatology?

When explaining her choice of Dermatology as a specialty, Dr. Otrofanowei highlighted her desire for long-term patient interaction and the generally better outcomes associated with the specialty as influencing factors.
“Dermatology is that specialty of Internal Medicine where I would say I am always certain I’m going to see my patients for a long time.”

She revealed an early inclination toward surgery: “As a medical student, I was surgically inclined. I wanted to use my hand and see the results of whatever it was I had done. I actually wanted to do urology.” However, as she got older, the commitment required by surgery began to weigh on her. “The training for surgical specialties is quite a long one, and it’s a very jealous specialty. Plus, I like the intrigue that internal medicine brings to the table, you just must think, evaluate and reason.”
For her, internal medicine is “the true bedrock of medicine,” offering the deep satisfaction of “piecing information together and forming a lovely story that can work for the patient.”
“So dermatology, for me, was a nice bridge of wanting to use my hands because I’m very big on procedural dermatology. I’m like, almost part surgery, part internal medicine.”

She also notes the close link to Genitourinary Medicine (GUM). “Genitourinary medicine is the sister of dermatology because a lot of the diseases of venereology, which is where it actually was coined from, present themselves on the skin. So you almost have no choice but to know GUM when you’re doing dermatology.”
One Humbling Patient Experience

When asked about a patient experience that shaped her approach, she stressed that each patient is unique. “The one thing that is common to all of us is that we are different. Patients are so different, and the way they reason through their problems is always amazing. That’s why empathy matters, putting yourself in their shoes.”

She eventually shared a humbling story: a man came in with a condition but felt he was too ‘educated, rich, and exposed’ to have it. Dr. Otrofanowei was concerned: “I was thinking, how do I break the news to this man? And how do I avoid being slapped?”

After a careful history and sensitive questions, she explained his diagnosis. He stormed out, hissing, “Nonsense.” His case was a blend of dermatology and genitourinary medicine, which meant issues of intimacy and sexual fidelity were involved.

“Well, unfortunately for him, he had to eat his humble pie. A week later, he came back because he was very uncomfortable, and on everyone’s advice. When he returned, I was proud of myself for pretending like nothing had happened. I simply went through the consultation again and said, ‘This is what I think has happened. These are the people that may or may not be involved; I will leave you to your humanity, to bring them in.’”

“That was humbling, because at the end of the day, he appreciated that I didn’t drive him away or tell him off. I was calm because I understood that this wasn’t just about his body; this was his ‘person’ that was almost being judged. It’s humbling when patients trust you with disclosures they’d rather keep between themselves and God. Hopefully, they are fortunate enough to have a doctor who understands the weight of that trust and holds it preciously.”
Defining Procedural Dermatology
A phrase Dr. Otrofanowei used earlier piqued our interest, so we asked her to explain what procedural dermatology really means.
“This is where we are hoping to break the myth or change the stereotype.
Dermatology isn’t just about creams or the old saying, ‘if it’s wet, dry it; if it’s dry, wet it.’

“That is not the beginning and end of dermatology at all. Dermatology is the specialty that deals with disorders of the skin and the entire integumentary system — hair, nails, and mucous membranes. In dermatology and genitourinary medicine, you often need to act quickly.”

She highlights the skin’s high visibility and its enormous impact on quality of life. “The skin is the largest organ of the body, and because it is so visible, problems with it affect people deeply… We have a lot of quick wins in dermatology. Some lesions have no systemic implications but still cause significant trouble by obstructing, being uncomfortable, or simply affecting how someone looks. And since you can’t really hide your skin, the impact on the quality of life is huge.”
“That’s where procedures come in. We cauterize or excise a lesion, use cryotherapy, or even remove an ingrown nail. These minor surgeries can make an immediate difference.”
Juggling Responsibilities: Balance and Priority
Being a consultant physician, lecturer, researcher, and board member is no easy feat. We asked Dr. Otrofanowei how she carries so much responsibility with grace.

“I always encourage people to try and be where they are happy. To do what they love and are gifted and trained to do. You find that adrenaline pushes you and makes you do a lot of things without you ‘seemingly’ feeling the effects. I say ‘seemingly’ in quotes, because when adrenaline is spent, exhaustion sets in.”

She emphasizes that achieving work-life balance is a deliberate choice, especially in fulfilling her various roles as a wife, mother, and more. “You have to be aware of what you want. You can’t drive your career so hard that your family suffers. But you also can’t define yourself only by your children. They will grow and leave, and you will not know what to do with yourself. Balance is intentional.”

The key, she adds, is learning to prioritize. “If your goal is always to do anything that you can do well, you break tasks down: What must be done now, what is important but less urgent, and what can wait. Your to-do list may never end, but if you’re clear on your priorities, you’ll give your best to what matters most.”

For medical students, she stresses the importance of a solid foundation. “If you cut corners in training, you won’t be able to build. Each new task will send you back to the basics. But if you’re properly grounded, every interaction adds to your growth.”

She also highlighted the role of curiosity in her research career. “You almost have no choice as a human being but to want to know more, and in any specialty, you soon realize that the more you know, the more you don’t know. It’s almost a lifelong act, but not a chore.”

On self-improvement, she advises: “You have to find what’s new. If you don’t take your time to improve yourself with what is new, you’ll be stale. Everybody’s going into artificial intelligence. AI is a tool, just like social media is a tool. But it shouldn’t replace you.
You must still know who you are, what you stand for, and what your goals are. Know what your stepping stones are, and you just keep climbing.”

She concludes with a message on failure: “Don’t look back thinking, I failed here. Yes, get up and move on. Because you must fail. Failing is not a prerequisite to winning, but if you haven’t hit any stumbling blocks, you might not appreciate what it is and develop the muscle to persevere and do better than you did the last time. It’s tough when you look at it just by yourself, but you have many helpers. Use your helpers.”
Skin Issues in Lagos vs. Global References
We asked Dr. Otrofanowei about common but overlooked skin issues in Lagos and whether they present differently compared to global references.

She immediately pointed to dry skin, which people often underestimate, as a trigger for more serious conditions. “Dry skin is usually itchy, and scratching breaks the skin’s protective barrier. That small break, combined with environmental factors, can lead to a cascade of problems that could have been avoided. Simple moisturizing makes a whole lot of difference.”

She also highlighted the rising prevalence of atopic dermatitis, which was once considered a disease of the affluent. “When I was younger, we used to say, ‘Atopic is for the white people and the rich. Dirty no dey kill African man.’ But the environment has changed.”

“And environment is not just the weather or geographical location. It’s how people dress, where they stay, and even their culture. How you prepare and eat your food. That’s all part of the environment. We’ve adopted Western habits, but we don’t live in a temperate climate. We can’t expect the same outcomes.”

Beyond personal skin habits, she drew attention to broader public health challenges. Pollution and overpopulation in Lagos are major culprits. “Whether you like it or not, the next person’s problems are going to impact you — how they live and dispose of things.

Lagos is struggling to be urban, but it isn’t. We’ve lost the rural protection of trees, greenery, and no cars or generators for pollution. The impact of pollution on skin disease is huge, and we have not even started unraveling it.”
Skin Myths and Misconceptions
On the common myths or misconceptions about skincare she often has to correct in her clinic.

She started by speaking to the influence of social media and foreign culture: “Unfortunately, Nigerians are not only Nigerians. Because we live in a ‘glocal’ world, the Nigerian is speaking with the influence of Koreans, Japanese and others.”
1. The Myth of ‘Glassy Skin’
The major misconception Dr. Otrofanowei addressed was the idea of ‘glassy skin’. She likes to narrow the skin’s functions down to three, using the acronym BED: Beauty, Excretion, and Defense.

“The beauty is all people think about. Meanwhile, the aesthetic of the skin will only be fully manifested when the excretory and the defensive functions are in order. Because beauty is actually from within… that is one saying that is literally true. Your skin reflects your inner health.”
Excretion: The skin helps with the excretion of sweat, urea, salt, and toxins — a natural cleansing process.

Defense: “The skin is a natural defense; it protects the external from going in and the internal from going out. This colour, this beautiful melanin that people want to remove and bleach out, is there for a reason.”

“Every time people try to scrape off something from the skin, by exfoliation or something else, they are also removing the natural protection that the skin gives by virtue of being alive. Your skin should have its own nice lubrication, which we call a natural moisturizing factor.”
2. Medicated Soaps and the Skin’s Vigilantes

Another misconception is the use of medicated or antibacterial soaps. “Everybody wants to use medicated soap or carrot soap to sanitize the skin. You should have normal bacteria on your skin as the owners. Their job is to protect you.
But when you use medicated soap, it doesn’t have sense to remove good bacteria from bad bacteria. So it takes away everything.”
And when a vigilante is out, armed robbers come in.

She expressed a strong disapproval of the obsession with facials and a one-size-fits-all approach to skincare: “The problem with this so-called skincare is we are doing one size fits all. That is the major issue, because you are not the same as the TikTok or Instagram influencers you are getting these advice from. Medicine is going to personalized care. Why would you follow a regimen that has no idea what you need?”
When we suggested that ‘glassy skin’ is just about a look — shiny and smooth — she was quick to clarify.

“The point is that when light hits a healthy skin that is free of textural defects, it will reflect. That glassy skin that you’re looking for, you got it. What you should be looking for is healthy skin.”
The pursuit of this look, she noted, often involves “50,000 layers of different types of oils and serums. It’s confusing the skin. It doesn’t understand what you’re trying to say.”
She boiled down good health down to a simple formula: Diet, Water, Sleep.
Sleep: “Sleep. I am guilty of not sleeping well, because I have so much work, but you have to take time off.”
Diet: “Eating well is an art. People just say eat well. They don’t really know what it means. Fruits in season are fantastic free radical busters.”
Water: “Water not soda or fizzy drinks. When your urine is clear, you know you’re drinking water. It’s the simple things, honestly.”
The Baseline Skincare Recommendation
We asked her for general skincare recommendation as a baseline for healthy skin and not just the face but the whole body.
“Well, honestly, it is so simple. It’s to cleanse, moisturize, and UV protect.”
1. Cleanse
“The only reason why you are cleansing is because the environment has interacted with your skin. And so what your skin has naturally produced… you need to cleanse.”
Do not strip the skin: The goal is to remove sweat and degrease without stripping off the body’s natural things.
Use simple, non-medicated soap: Dr. Otrofanowei recommends synthetic detergents over traditional soap, as soap is alkaline and raises the skin’s natural acidic pH (4.5 to 5.5).
“We would rather you didn’t do that. But because most soaps are not synthetic detergents, if you soap, moisturize so that your skin can come back through a pseudo acidic Ph.”

Hair and Scalp: “Your hair needs water, moisture… at least once a week, because you can have water on your hair without necessarily soaping it or shampooing it. That moisture is good and then you just trap it with some oils.”
2. Moisturize
The idea of a moisturizer is to trap water.

Apply to damp skin: “We always tell people after you’ve cleansed your skin, don’t towel dry. Let there still be some water on your skin so that when you apply the emollient, it traps water and improves the moisture content of the skin.”

Emollients (Vehicles): “Lotions (lighter, less water) are lighter than creams, and creams are lighter than ointments. Ointments and oils have little to no water, so you should use them to seal in existing water on the skin.”
“Every part of your skin should be moisturized, both the parts you see and you don’t see.”
3. UV Protection (Sun Protect)

UV protection is necessary primarily for photoaging (photoheliosis). “A lot of people don’t want to grow old. You may look younger or healthy. It’s not a wrong thing to pursue. But honestly, it’s just these three, cleanse, moisturize, photo protect.”
Dr. Otrofanowei recommends the 5 S’s of UV Protection:
Slip on long-sleeved clothing for protection.
Slop on the sunscreen.
Slap on a hat.
Seek shade.
Slide on sunglasses, as you also have melanocytes in the eyes that need photoprotection.

Our “Dear Future Doctor” series took a brief hiatus, but like a well-rested clinician returning to the wards, we are back and more energized than ever. We know you’ve missed these deep dives into the minds of the mentors shaping Nigerian medicine. Today, we finally resume our conversation with the inimitable Dr. Erere Otrofanowei.

If Part 1 was an introduction to the world of dermatology, Part 2 is the clinical rotation you didn’t know you needed. We’re moving beyond the surface to discuss the politics of sunscreen, the “Japa” syndrome, and why the stethoscope of a dermatologist must be backed by the sharpest internal medicine brain in the building.
Grab your ward coats; the clinic is back in session.
Beyond the Glow: The UV Safety Manifesto

We often hear the phrase “Black don’t crack,” a cultural badge of honor for our melanin-rich skin. But Dr. Otrofanowei is quick to pivot the conversation from “sun safety” to the more precise UV safety. While our Caucasian counterparts face higher rates of melanoma than we do, because of the protection melanin provides. Our struggle in the Nigerian context is often different, yet equally important.

“I’m glad you said UV safety as opposed to sun safety,” she begins, noting that we definitely need precautions. The primary culprit? Photoheliosis. While we might not see the same frequency of sun-induced skin cancers, photoheliosis, which is the damage from photoaging, is a constant.

“Because if you don’t prevent what you know is going to happen, you’ll be using many things to fix it,” she warns. Even the types of skin cancers that are more local to us, like squamous cell carcinomas, are exacerbated when present on sun-exposed areas of the skin.”

The “glocal” nature of life now means that Nigerians often hear global advice and take it “hook, line, and sinker” without local context. What Dr. Otrofanowei sees in her clinic are patients struggling with melasma, dermatosis papulosa nigrans, and pigmentation disorders — often the result of untreated photo damage or attempts to “bleach away” the very protection nature gave us.
“You don’t have to fix what could have been prevented in the first place.”

Her advice for us? Start with the basics. UV safety isn’t just about using expensive creams to block the sun’s effect. We also need to be protected from the High Energy Visible Light (HEVL) emitted by our phones, tablets, and even spotlights. And the simple act of moisturizing provides a barrier in its most basic form. She also reminds us to look at our plates: “Let food be your medicine… Let your plate have the colors of the rainbow. Literally. In its purest form. Chances are, your skin would repair itself before it needs extra products. And if you do need extra help, it will respond quickly to it”.
The Sunscreen Gap: A Policy of Protection

We discussed the data of some studies she coauthored that had jarring disparities in the statistics: while 70% of medical students know about sunscreen, less than 30% use it. And in another study among Lagos traders, awareness drops to 10%.

Why the gap? “Sunscreen is costly,” she admits, “but it’s only costly because it has been taken as a beauty thing, as opposed to a useful, regular product.” The beauty industry has capitalized on the “glow,” but the medical reality is different.
“We are even trying to get people to moisturize regularly first. Just moisturize regularly.”
Dermatologists are currently working with the WHO to push for urea as a compound in emollients. Dr. Otrofanowei calls it a fantastic, hygroscopic tool for hydration and atopic patients.
But she challenges us to think beyond the bottle. If a person can’t afford sunscreen, can they seek shade? Can they wear lightweight long-sleeved cotton clothes? Use an umbrella? Wear a hat?

“The problem is the attitude and the practice,” she notes. If medical students who know better aren’t doing better, what do we expect from the public? The push must shift from just “sunscreen” to comprehensive UV protection.

The “Skinese” of Advocacy and Education When asked how medical educators could incorporate UV safety in community outreaches, she admitted that for the medical educators, the challenge is getting a ‘buy-in’. “Many of them might not even believe in the importance of UV protection themselves.” Dermatology is often dismissed as a “female thing” or a purely cosmetic field. Dr. Otrofanowei points out the irony: “The Presidents of the Nigerian Association of Dermatology and even the International Society of Dermatologists are men… so why are we losing our menfolk to push certain narratives?”

“To change the culture, we have to go where the people are. That means moving beyond the ‘1 million likes’ on social media, which in reality, reaches only a select few in Nigeria… and returning to radio jingles, TV, and community outreach. Medical educators are not necessarily specialists; we also have to reach the GPs, nurses, and pharmacists. People who have primary contact with members of the community. It also means refining our curriculum. Currently, in some medical schools, many students only get a two-week exposure to dermatology at the 600 level, a far cry from the three-month junior postings of the past.’’

The Digital Shift: Telemedicine and dermatology As the world pivots toward digital solutions, the question of tele-dermatology in Nigeria has become a necessity. Dr. Otrofanowei notes that its rising popularity is born out of a shortage of specialists. “It’s gaining popularity because all the ones we’re training are going outside,” she explains, noting that with her own frequent travels, incorporating telemedicine is no longer optional. “We have no choice but to incorporate telemedicine. We have no choice.” While she was practicing it pre-COVID, the post-pandemic era has made it even more “pertinent” in a global shortage of dermatologists.
“Dermatology is a very difficult specialty if you want to do it right. Your internal medicine knowledge has to be sound.”
However, she worries that the current medical curriculum hinders this growth.

“You guys don’t have early exposure to dermatology. Before you get to dermatology posting, other specialties would have caught your interest,” she points out, contrasting the current two-week exposure at the 600 level with the three-month junior posting she received during her own training. This lack of exposure doesn’t just reduce interest among students; it allows misinformation to flourish among the public. “That’s where you guys come in,” she says, charging the next generation to help change the narrative and correct the lies being spread about skin health.

Doctors vs. Influencers: An Ethical Divide This information gap often leads patients into the wrong hands. Dr. Otrofanowei recalls a story of a young lady who sought a ‘dermatologist’ at a local beauty shop. After following the advice of these so-called dermatologists, she developed further skin complications that finally landed her in a real medical clinic.

The idea that anyone would believe that a medical doctor would consult in a beauty store is something Dr. Otrofanowei finds deeply affronting; it is, as she puts it, ‘basically going to the market to look for a doctor’. But why aren’t the real experts louder online? The answer lies in professional ethics.
The Ethos of Silence: Unlike beauty influencers, doctors are bound by professional ethics that prevent them from “trending” through negativity or maligning others.
No Advertising: A dermatologist cannot post “I am the best, come and see me”. To do so would be to risk their medical license.
The “Loudness” Myth: Dr. Otrofanowei reminds us that medicine is not a loud profession. “The fact that you don’t know dermatology does not make us quiet; it just shows that you are ignorant.”

She argues that the information is available for anyone willing to spend “0.001 seconds to search online”. While social media platforms like Instagram and TikTok are popular, they aren’t the primary home for a physician. “I’m not supposed to be there,” she concludes. “If I’m there, how will I be in the clinic?”

Blooming Where You Are Planted: The Japa Dialogue We couldn’t have a “Dear Future Doctor” episode in 2026 without discussing the “Japa” syndrome. Dr. Otrofanowei’s stance is firm, Christian, and very patriotic.

“I am fully African. I’m Nigerian. I don’t even want to give anybody else any credit. I’m also a Christian, and I believe that anywhere you’re at is where you are supposed to be at the time you are at it,” she says. Drawing inspiration from Professor Bode’s inaugural lecture, she encourages us to “bloom where you are planted.”

She isn’t against international exposure. In fact, she encourages networking and ‘conquering’ states and continents. Of expanding your mind beyond your current reality, even if it means leaving your state to do your house job and youth service elsewhere. “It’s not even necessarily about leaving Nigeria.”

But she warns against the mindset that success requires leaving. “If your mind has already closed itself to saying, ‘it cannot be done here,’ trust me, it cannot be done. People are doing well here; take time to ask them how they achieved what they had; you will be surprised at what you will gain. We are always trying to project ourselves based on another person’s story. Create your own path.”

She also speaks to the ‘ripple effect’ of the brain drain. When doctors leave, they leave behind classmates to fix the problems they walked away from. “Once you remove yourself from the equation, you don’t have the mouth to talk again,” she says bluntly. For those who remain, the fear is real: “I’m looking at all the people that I’m part of training, and they’re leaving, and I’m thinking, ‘who’s going to take care of me?’”

“God did not make a mistake putting you where you are. My honest thought on the whole Japa thing is that if you don’t know who you are, whether you leave or stay, you will always be floundering. You need to know who you are and what you stand for.”
A Career in “Skinese”: Advice for the Aspiring

If you are considering dermatology, Dr. Otrofanowei has one requirement: Love it. Don’t choose it because skincare is trending. Choose it because you have a fundamental, principled reason for being there.

“In medicine, please love whatever it is you want to do… the chances are that you’re going to succeed and excel there because it’s not a chore.” And while money is a tool, she advises against making it the primary goal. “If you only ask for money, you will use the money to solve the many problems that you have. Instead, ask God for what you truly need so that whether you have money or you don’t have money, you have the things that you need.”

Medicine is a vast field; it’s not just clinical; there is medical education, policy, medical law, and molecular medicine. Don’t limit yourself; there is so much you can become. But whatever it is that you want to do… make sure you love it.

“Be like a sponge,” she urges us. “Take it all. Be universal. Let the school pass through you, and you pass through the school. Be fully present in every posting, and when you come out, you can make a fully informed decision.”
“In derm, the harvest is plenty, but the laborers are few. Please come. Male, female. Join us in dermatology.”
The Final Word

Dr. Otrofanowei leaves us with a challenge: “Do your own part in your little corner and just try to make a positive impact in everything you do. Don’t look to please others or for man’s vain glory because you can never please men. God has given you a talent for something, whether you stay or go, whether you choose the clinic or elsewhere, find your purpose. And leave positive ripple effects.”

Every year in September, we remember the ones whose pain made another breath feel unbearable. We have talks, hold campaigns, and create a societal awareness of the need to slow down and look in the eyes of the person next to you, and maybe give them a hug while you’re at it.

The word suicide often feels forbidden, one that should not be uttered, especially in our cultural context. Perhaps this is why the frustrated father or the overwhelmed medical student who has considered suicide is too scared to ask for help. Because nobody wants to be seen as weak, different, or broken.

Changing the narrative on suicide means breaking the silence, redefining the conversation, and challenging the stigma that surrounds it. It means reminding ourselves that sometimes, we all need a little help- someone to walk with us and remind us that we are not alone.

It’s often said that a problem shared is a problem half solved. The point is to highlight the power of speaking out. In reality, this is easier said than done; there is a culture of shame that might position a person as the subject of community gossip within two market days of them speaking up. The sudden awkward silence, hushed whispers, and pointed stares. Yet, even in such moments, someone safe and true is waiting to listen. Speaking out isn’t shameful; it’s a show of immense strength.
Dying in silence only worsens the wound. It makes a gaping hole wider, and it robs humanity of a treasure.

There is another popular saying intended to inspire optimism: There is light at the end of the tunnel. But what happens when the tunnel feels dark and endless? When the brief flicker of hope fans out like fire under rain?

Shifting the narrative means not standing on the sidelines telling people to keep going, but holding their hand and walking with them until the light appears. It’s creating safe spaces when needed and seeking professional help because there’s nothing wrong with needing therapy. No tunnel, however long, lasts forever. Light always comes, and until it does, your story is still unfolding- one page, one breath at a time.

To the one struggling to get through the tunnel, there are trusted people- friends, mentors, communities, even organizations- who will not weaponize your pain. A name might come to mind as you read this; do not be afraid to let them hold your hand.

Life comes with its own share of obstacles distributed in different measures. But in isolation, it might often look like some obstacles are impossible to overcome. This is a lie because the breath in our lungs is a symbol of hope.
In.
Out.

The rise and fall of your chest is a sign of life. Life that is yours to choose. A powerful proof that you are still here. Choose it fervently because you deserve colors and vibrancy in this world. We are all living life for the first time; nobody has it all figured out, even if it looks like they do.

To the ones who are in a position to hold another’s hand. You need to understand that your words and actions can either sap or save a life. You have a choice, and you can choose to be gracious. There has to be a conscious effort to be your ‘brother’s keeper.’

Suicide prevention doesn’t end in September, and when the buzz dies down, our awareness shouldn’t. It’s a kind smile and a compliment. It’s the “how are you?” Not to tick a perfunctory box but because you actually care. It’s the random check-ins and phone conversations. Tell that boy you admire his strength; remind your friend that they matter.

To the ones fighting silent battles, you will not become a statistic on our watch. Even in the darkest nights, stars still burn. Let this article be a reminder that you are seen, you are loved, you are cared for, and you are prayed for. You matter more than you know, and your tomorrow is worth waiting for.
Suicide prevention is a culture we build, one act of kindness at a time. The light at the end of the tunnel may feel far away, but together we carry lanterns.
May our words heal, may our presence strengthen, and may our compassion keep the flame alive- until no one has to walk the tunnel alone.

I realized that contributing to knowledge is as good, if not even more fulfilling as actually looking after the women one-on-one.

Professor Bosede Bukola Afolabi is undeniably a force to be reckoned with. A distinguished obstetrician and gynecologist, she is renowned for her contributions to maternal and fetal medicine. She serves as a Consultant at the Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) and was Head of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at the College of Medicine, University of Lagos from 2018 till 2021.

With a medical degree from Obafemi Awolowo University and a Doctorate in Medicine from the University of Nottingham, her expertise spans clinical practice, research, and academia. She is also the Director of the Centre for Clinical Trials, Research and Implementation Science (CCTRIS) and founder of the Maternal and Reproductive Health Research Collective (MRHRC).

Professor Afolabi has led several impactful research initiatives, many supported by international bodies such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, particularly in improving outcomes for pregnant women living with sickle cell disease and advancing reproductive health in Nigeria.

When we walked into her beautifully curated office, it was easy to sense her eye for detail. Every artwork and element of the decor reflected the same precision and intentionality she brings to her work. She welcomed us with a brisk, businesslike tone, letting us know we had just five minutes. But those five minutes quickly stretched into a thirty-minute, power-packed conversation rich with wisdom, candor, and the kind of clarity that can only come from a life steeped in purpose.

Professor Afolabi is warm, witty, and fiercely intelligent- traits that shine through in this conversation about her journey, her philosophy, and her unwavering commitment to improving women’s health in Nigeria.

The interview consisted of two interviewers from the AMSUL Editorial Board and Prof. Afolabi, the interviewee. This interview has been edited for clarity and flow, but every effort has been made to preserve the authenticity of Prof. Afolabi’s voice and perspectives.
Her Motivations And Early Experiences.

“My main motivations were a natural flair in medical school for the subject and some extremely dedicated lecturers that we had in Ife at the time who sank Obstetrics and Gynecology into our brains. We also did Obstetrics and Gynecology for six months in I believe the senior posting. As opposed to how it’s done here when it’s just for about three or four months over two years, this was a complete stretch of six months.”

Being a woman herself, she also found it easy to empathize with other women. “I have experienced a lot of the symptoms that they complain about, I’m able to relate better, and I really enjoy looking after women.”

Talking about her early experience during residency, she admits that she initially believed research to be a chore. “I got to appreciate the beauty of research towards the end of my training. I trained in the UK, and at first, I didn’t know why anybody had to add to the stress of residency by also doing research. Isn’t it stressful enough?”

It wasn’t until her third year of training in the UK that her perspective changed. She discovered that contributing to knowledge could be as fulfilling , sometimes even more so , than one-on-one care. “So with those learnings and experiences, it made me decide to become a clinician and a scientist.”
Wearing Many Hats: What Came Naturally — and What Surprised Her

“I think being a clinician came most naturally to me, strangely enough. Medical school is tough, and you’re always second-guessing yourself. But once I started specializing, everything came naturally. Within six months, I was doing caesarean sections, vacuum, forceps, you know. And we mustn’t forget that O&G is not just procedures. It’s also about really looking after women. So that came quite naturally to me.”

“Leadership also came naturally to me. I’m quite organized and have good people skills, if I say so myself, so people enjoy working with me and often want to keep working with me. I found I had a flair for that as well.”

“Being a researcher is probably the one that was surprising because, like I said, at the beginning, I wondered why anybody wanted to go through that stress, and also because you have to train hard to learn how to do research properly.
I had some natural skills for it, but it was more difficult. I wouldn’t say it surprised me, but it is more difficult to get into properly.”
Her natural flair for leadership prompted us to ask if she was a course rep at any point in medical school, but with a laugh, she told us that she wasn’t.
A Researcher for a Cause

Her research has deeply impacted maternal health, particularly in women with sickle cell disease. What drew her into that area was a desire for excellence and building meaningful work. She was inspired by her mentor, Professor Olalekan Abudu, a former head of department and former provost of the college, whose earlier bench research laid the foundation. “I wanted to answer the questions his work raised. And this is where we have the highest number of people in that area (sickle cell). I felt that affinity to them and wanted to help make them better.”

When asked about the real-world impact of her research. She visibly lit up speaking about her ongoing research on sickle cell in pregnancy. “We started with basic science research, first of all, what are the possible mechanisms for their not having such successful pregnancies? Is it just because of the sickle cell itself, or are there other things or other reasons related to their physiology?”
“We did all those physiological research, found certain things, and kept moving forward.

So most likely to impact the real world now is the one to do with ‘aspirin versus placebo’ that we just completed in sickle cell pregnancy, and unfortunately, I can’t tell you about it yet because we haven’t published, but it’s going to make an impact.”
Her Approach To Leadership And Mentorship.
As a former Head of Department and current Director of CCTRIS, her leadership philosophy is simple:
“I approach leadership in a humane manner. My goal is to improve the environment, both for the residents and my colleagues. And for CCTRIS, I aim to make it more visible, relevant, and active.
One thing I’m very deliberate about is not being political. I focus on output and merit, not forming cliques or taking sides.
For example, the resident doctors who show that they are really hardworking and want to do more are given the tools to be able to do more.

I was also very particular about creating a mentorship program, such that people were paired with people they wanted to be mentored by. They had first, second, and third choices of people they wanted to mentor them and then pairing them and trying to ensure that people got mentored.”
“I’m very, very deliberate about bringing up people that work with me and under me.”

“At the end of the day, you can’t do everything. And it’s important to try and give people opportunities that you have, make them succeed, and if possible, even get higher. There are several PhD students who are getting really great at doing research, and it helps make the department better and helps make CCTRIS itself better.
And I delegate, I don’t micromanage. I let people run with things. So that’s my style generally; non-micromanaging, mentoring, and trying to make people develop capacity to a large extent.”
Approaching Sensitive Topics Like Contraceptives, Abortion And Infertility.
“They are definitely sensitive — but I think it’s more religion-based than cultural. And my approach is always to ask: What’s the endgame?
The reality is that maternal mortality is worse when abortion and contraception are restricted.”
“And my main reason for being a clinician is that I want women to survive pregnancy and childbirth. I don’t want them to die.”
“I think religion should not rule the state. In my view, it should be individual or family-based. It shouldn’t dictate public policy, especially policies that affect other people’s lives and choices.

It is clear that everywhere in the world, when abortion is heavily restricted, women die. They resort to unsafe methods, they hide, and they die. And women are the only ones who can get pregnant. Nobody else goes through that. So, despite all the abstinence campaigns, there is no setting where abstinence alone has worked 100%. It just doesn’t.

If we want to save women’s lives, we need to be more liberal about abortion laws. The same goes for contraception. The more women get pregnant, the more they’re likely to die because of pregnancy and childbirth. So it’s important to space families and allow women to be able to do so and make decisions about their own bodies.”
On Japa and Responsibility
Her take on the japa syndrome is layered.
“I japa’d too- but with an intention to return.”

“I was so clear about it. I was so sure when I was leaving and even before I left that I was coming back. Such that as soon as I finished my training, I came back. I did what I planned to do. And it was within five years.”

Her goal was to specialize quickly, return to Nigeria, and rise through the ranks. “I wanted to be a professor before 40.” She laughed, “I was very much in a hurry when I was younger, I don’t know why. I entered medical school at 15.”

“I came back and entered the system because I wanted to make the system work. In Ife, I think by my second year there, I met some people whose whole plan was always very ‘we must make Nigeria better,’ and all those things. I was so left-wing then, the people that I admired most were all these Marxist professors who drove Beetle. Now, I don’t think that it is, what’s it called, to not have money. But I still very much believe in making the system better.”
She sympathizes with today’s challenges:

“It’s not as if I don’t understand the reasons behind it. I know that things are difficult here for a doctor, especially one that’s just starting. You don’t earn a lot of money or a lot of experience in terms of the sort of equipment that are available in some areas, not in all.
We also don’t have programs that are so very well structured that they are always follow to the T. It’s a problem.”
But she’s concerned that young doctors don’t feel responsible for the country anymore. “We also don’t have that mentality anymore of feeling responsible for an environment.
This is your country. You don’t have any other country.
It’s as if we feel that we owe no responsibility at all to this country, and we just have to go and do things for ourselves.

I don’t know if it’s the generation. We tend to say these Gen Zs and Millennials are so into themselves. But I also feel that there must be some things we need to learn from you. Every generation always feels the younger ones coming after them are rubbish.
But I don’t believe that, I think that your independence helps you. That inward looking manner also helps in ways some of us are still yet to totally realize.”

“But back to the question itself, Japa has now become a fashion, people don’t even think about it anymore. Just finish and go. And that realization of what it is doing to the country, how it’s making things even worse, is not there. Nobody seems to see it or care about it. That is what worries me.”

“A lot of people have relatives that are still here. Those relatives will be helping you japa meanwhile, they will fall ill. They need care, but the care is not available because all of you have left.

You can’t move all of Nigeria abroad. I don’t know how it’s going to how it can be done, whether there should be structured ‘rejapa’ programs. But as we go, the same country you are complaining about gets worse in every way, it doesn’t get better.
And it’s only yourselves that get better. You also make another system get better.”
“Your education was hideously subsidized at the detriment of the country, and then we take that to places where to train a doctor is about ten times what’s paid, if not more.”
“So it just doesn’t balance, it is important that you people also think about that.
Maybe form organizations where it’s not just about you, you have to start thinking about how to change things back to improve the system, and think about it in a very structured manner.”
Lessons for the Future Doctor
When asked what lessons she hopes future doctors take to heart, her answer is clear:
“Be a lifelong learner. Medicine changes all the time — and if you don’t keep up, you’ll harm your patients, or worse, face legal trouble.”
“It’s very common for older doctors to get stuck in that rot of not reading regularly and updating themselves and doing older things.

Then when people start talking about the evidence, they dismiss it saying we have to still do our own studies. I mean, yes, we do have to do our own studies, but there are things being developed all the time that you need to be abreast of, in order to practice properly, more efficiently, and more legally. Because when legalese things come up, you have to go back to the evidence to be sure that you did the right thing.”

She also emphasizes the need to speak up. “Medicine is hierarchical. It’s important for you to speak up. As females in particular, but even as young doctors as well, we tend to keep quiet and not say things that we should. Whether it’s to do with clinical or even your general professional development, you need to speak up.

You can be respectful and still speak up. I can’t know everything, the lowest level of evidence is expert opinion. I may be wrong, I may not be abreast of the current evidence. You can save a patient’s life by speaking up.”
To Those Considering O&G — and Whether to Japa or Stay.
Finally, she offers advice to young doctors choosing between staying and going, especially those eyeing a career in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
“Residency here, I feel is still okay in some institutions. When you’re doing your residency, the beauty of the world now is that there’s so much available online. There’s so much you can learn.

And even if you decide to stay, you can go out for programs, you can go out for one-year or six-month programs where you can specialize more. There are subspecializations in almost every condition, especially O & G. We started doing maternal and fetal medicine and so on.
You can learn all these things here, and you can better yourself very easily. In fact, right now, the US is getting less attractive, especially with the current situation there.

But global health is still a big deal and funds are still coming to us here to do better work, research. There are all sorts of different clinical opportunities. So you can stay, get yourselves into some of these things and improve yourselves that way. In terms of japaing, I think one of the ways is to have a time frame to do whatever it is want to do and come back, so that you can set up something or join the system one way or the other.
There’s still so many different skills that are needed here.”
“When you japa you are one in hundred million but when you stay here you can make a big difference.”
“So I think that that is some of the advice I’d give you.”

Professor Afolabi’s journey is a testament of what happens when passion meets purpose. From Ife to the UK and back again, her life challenges the next generation of doctors to stay curious, stay committed, and consider the bigger picture.
